step1_summary: Chief complaint: 5-day history of worsening dry cough and continuously streaming nose.

Symptom details: Dry cough every 20–30 min; no sputum, haemoptysis or chest pain; no dyspnoea. Rhinorrhoea described as “pretty green.” Subjective fever with alternating chills; has not measured temperature. Myalgias present. Brief self-limited diarrhoea at onset. No sore throat, ear pain, headache, visual changes, or rash. Symptoms somewhat soothed by 2–3 sachets/day of Lemsip (paracetamol-containing cold remedy).
Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension. No chronic lung disease.
Medications: Metformin (dose not stated). Lisinopril (patient believes “200,” likely 20 mg). PRN Lemsip. No regular glucose monitoring mentioned.
Allergies: None to drugs; occasional mild hay-fever.
Family/social: Lives with partner and dog. Office manager. Denies regular smoking; drinks only the “odd sherry.”
Vital signs / exam: None recorded (remote visit). No reported dyspnoea, wheeze, or chest findings.
Labs/imaging: Routine diabetes bloods 3 weeks ago reportedly ‘normal.’ No current labs or imaging.

V: Pulmonary embolism: Acute cough and subjective fever could occur, but absence of dyspnoea, chest pain or risk factors make it less likely.
I: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold, influenza, COVID-19): Most common cause of acute cough + rhinorrhoea + myalgias/fever for 5 days.
Acute viral bronchitis: Extension of URI to lower airway can give persistent dry cough without sputum or dyspnoea.
Acute bacterial sinusitis: Green nasal discharge, facial congestion; could follow viral illness.
N: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma: Can cause persistent nasal discharge, but time-course too acute.
D: Exacerbation of chronic obstructive airway disease (unlikely given no history).
I2: ACE-inhibitor–induced cough (lisinopril): Dry cough common with ACEIs.
C: Cystic fibrosis carrier state (unlikely with adult presentation and minimal past infections).
A: Allergic rhinitis: Watery rhinorrhoea, nasal itching, cough from post-nasal drip.
T: Inhaled foreign body/irritant exposure: Could trigger cough but not rhinorrhoea or fever.
E: Uncontrolled diabetes-related immunosuppression predisposing to infection (contributor rather than diagnosis).

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold or influenza-like illness)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Most typical cause of simultaneous dry cough, rhinorrhoea, myalgias and subjective fever starting abruptly over 5 days in an otherwise healthy adult.
supporting_evidence: No focal chest findings or purulent sputum.
opposing_evidence: Greenish nasal discharge could suggest bacterial component (though color alone not specific).
Patient is diabetic, raising concern for bacterial infection progression.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Current epidemiology makes SARS-CoV-2 a common viral cause of acute cough, feverishness and myalgias; symptoms overlap with common cold/influenza.
supporting_evidence: Diabetes is a risk factor for infection and complications.
opposing_evidence: No anosmia, ageusia, or dyspnoea reported.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute bacterial sinusitis with post-viral component
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Green nasal discharge, facial pressure description, and >5 days of persistent symptoms can indicate bacterial super-infection following viral URI.
supporting_evidence: Persistence beyond usual 3–4 days of viral peak.
opposing_evidence: Lack of facial pain/tenderness or foul odor.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dry cough is a classic side-effect; however onset usually weeks–months after starting drug and would not explain nasal symptoms, myalgias or fever.
opposing_evidence: Cough began acutely 5 days ago after likely viral prodrome.
Concurrent rhinorrhoea and systemic symptoms not explained by ACEI.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Watery rhinorrhoea and cough can be allergic, but systemic feverish feelings and myalgias favor infectious etiology.
opposing_evidence: Subjective fever/chills and myalgias atypical for simple allergy.
Acute time-limited onset not linked to specific allergen exposure.
